summary: Keystone grazer of the Serengeti–Mara; over a million animals follow the rains in a clockwise annual migration.
identification: Slate-grey to silver body with dark vertical stripes on the neck and flanks
Black beard and mane; both sexes carry curved, cow-like horns
Sloping back: shoulders noticeably higher than the hindquarters
Usually in large herds; calving peak Jan–Mar on the southern short-grass plains
habitat: Open short-grass plains and acacia savanna, close to water.
field_action: Estimate herd size in bands of 10/50/100. Note river crossings and calving sites.

summary: Moves with and slightly ahead of the wildebeest migration, cropping taller grass.
identification: Broad black-and-white stripes that extend under the belly
Faint 'shadow stripes' between the black stripes on the haunches
Erect mane; stocky horse-like build
Family groups of a stallion with several mares and foals
habitat: Grasslands and open woodland; never far from water.
lookalikes: Grévy's zebra (narrow stripes, white belly; not in this ecosystem)
field_action: Record group size and foals present.

summary: Largest land mammal and an ecosystem engineer that shapes woodland and grassland balance.
identification: Very large ears shaped like the African continent
Concave back; two finger-like tips at the end of the trunk
Both sexes usually carry tusks
Matriarchal herds; adult bulls often alone or in bachelor groups
habitat: Savanna, riverine forest and escarpment woodland; seasonal movement to water.
field_action: Keep at least 50 m away. Record herd composition and any injuries, snares or carcasses immediately.

summary: Social apex predator living in prides with defended territories.
identification: Tawny, unpatterned coat; black tail tuft
Adult males have a mane, which darkens with age
Round ears with black backs
Usually seen resting in groups during the day
habitat: Open plains and woodland edge, often near kopjes and water.
field_action: Photograph whisker-spot patterns to identify individuals. Report collared animals with their collar ID.

summary: Tallest browser; its population fell by about half over three generations.
identification: Jagged, star- or vine-leaf-shaped dark patches
Patches extend down the legs to the hooves
Two to three ossicones; males bald on top
lookalikes: Reticulated giraffe (smooth-edged polygons; not in this ecosystem)
field_action: Photograph the left flank square-on for pattern-based individual ID.

summary: Browsing rhino reduced to small, intensively protected populations.
identification: Pointed, prehensile upper lip used for browsing
Two horns; head usually held up
Smaller ears than the white rhino; no shoulder hump
Calf runs behind its mother (in front in white rhino)
habitat: Dense bush, thickets and woodland edges.
lookalikes: White rhino (square lip, prominent hump; grazes)
field_action: Do not approach. Report the sighting to the rhino monitoring unit by radio. Do not share locations publicly.

summary: Highly social, wide-ranging pack hunter; one of Africa's most endangered carnivores.
identification: Mottled coat of black, tan, yellow and white, unique to each animal
Large rounded ears
White-tipped bushy tail
Packs of 6–20; very active at dawn and dusk
habitat: Open plains and woodland; packs range over hundreds of km².
lookalikes: Spotted hyena (sloping back, small rounded spots)
field_action: Photograph both flanks of every individual. Report denning behaviour immediately.

summary: High-flying scavenger collapsing because of poisoning and loss of nesting cliffs.
identification: Scaly-looking plumage: dark feathers with pale edges
Yellowish bill; long, sparsely feathered neck
In flight, rows of white spots on the underwing coverts
habitat: Open savanna; nests colonially on cliffs and gorges.
field_action: Multiple dead vultures may indicate poisoning. Do not touch carcasses; report immediately.

summary: Aggressive ornamental escapee forming dense, toxic thickets that displace native grazing.
identification: Square, prickly stems; scrambling shrub 1–3 m tall
Rough, toothed leaves with a pungent smell when crushed
Flat-topped clusters of small flowers that change colour (yellow→orange→pink)
Glossy black berries in clusters
habitat: Disturbed ground, lodge gardens, drainage lines and woodland edges.
lookalikes: Native Lippia (no prickles, aromatic, white-pink flowers)
field_action: Map the infestation edge, not just its centre. Estimate cover (%) in the notes.

summary: Fast-spreading annual that is toxic to livestock and causes dermatitis; spreads along roads.
identification: Deeply lobed, pale-green leaves forming a basal rosette
Many small white flower heads, about 4 mm across, each with 5 tiny 'petals'
Upright plant 0.5–1.5 m tall with hairy, grooved stems
habitat: Roadsides, gravel pits, overgrazed and disturbed soil.
field_action: Wear gloves; do not pull plants that are flowering. Log the furthest plant along each road.

summary: Cactus spread by baboons and elephants; its spines injure wildlife mouths and feet.
identification: Flat, oval, blue-green pads (cladodes)
Few long yellowish spines; tufts of fine glochids
Yellow flowers; purple-red pear-shaped fruit
habitat: Dry rocky slopes, kopjes and degraded rangeland.
lookalikes: Euphorbia candelabrum (native, ribbed stems, milky latex)
field_action: Note fruiting status and whether it is spreading through animal dung.

summary: Thorny tree forming impenetrable stands that lower water tables and suppress grasses.
identification: Twice-pinnate, feathery leaves with small leaflets
Paired straight thorns at the nodes
Yellow catkin-like flower spikes; long, straw-coloured, curved pods
habitat: Riverbanks, floodplains and settlements in drier areas.
lookalikes: Native Vachellia/Acacia (round or flat pods, often white thorns)
field_action: Record stand size and whether seedlings are present downstream.
